43.title: The overflowing cup
43.hook: the master Nan-in pours tea for a professor until it spills: you are already full (Zen story, Japan)
43.howItsDone: Some Zen teachers start new students with beginner's mind, shoshin, and the cup of tea story is told in Zen centers and beyond them to describe coming to practice without assuming you already understand.

segments.voice: Yesterday: it's the donkey. A guard searched the straw for years and never looked at the animal. Today, a new week: Zen stories.

A university professor has come to call on a Zen master named Nan-in. The story sets it in Japan, in the Meiji era. The professor wants to learn about Zen, and he has a lot to say about it. He's read the books. He has theories. He talks, and talks. Nan-in says almost nothing. He makes tea, sets a cup in front of the professor, and begins to pour. The cup fills to the brim. Nan-in keeps pouring. Tea runs over the rim, across the table, onto the floor.
screen: `A PROFESSOR COMES TO LEARN.` → `HE TALKS, AND TALKS.` → `THE MASTER KEEPS POURING.`

segments.voice: The professor can't stand it. Stop, he says, it's full! Nothing more will go in! Nan-in puts the pot down. That's you, he says, more or less: like this cup, full of your own opinions. How can I show you anything until you empty it first? That's the whole story: a teapot, a cup, and a puddle on the floor. A word about where it comes from. It reached English readers through a twentieth-century collection of Zen stories, and its earlier history in Japan is hard to trace, so hold it as a teaching story, not a court record. What it teaches is simple and hard: you can't learn what you think you already know. The professor didn't come to learn. He came to be confirmed. Anything new Nan-in might have said would have spilled off the top of what was already there. Zen has a word for the opposite state: shoshin, beginner's mind. The Japanese teacher Shunryu Suzuki, who taught in America, built his talks around it, teaching that a beginner sees many possibilities where an expert sees few. Emptying the cup doesn't mean throwing away everything you know. It means leaving room: room for the other person to surprise you, room for a subject you think you've mastered to still have something to say. The cup is only useful for the space inside it.

Sit with that cup in front of you, and breathe. Think of one subject, or one person, you're sure you already understand, and leave a little room at the top.

44.title: Two monks and a river
44.hook: Tanzan carries a woman across a stream, and hours later Ekido is still carrying her in his head (Zen story, Japan)
44.carry: I set her down at the river
44.howItsDone: Zen teachers tell the story of Tanzan and Ekido when talking about letting go, and in meditation practice people notice a thought they keep returning to and set it down, again and again.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was shoshin, beginner's mind: Nan-in poured tea until it spilled. Your line was empty the cup.

Two in the morning. Someone lies awake replaying a remark from lunch. Or from last week. Or from years ago. The person who said it has long forgotten it, and is fast asleep. And the remark is still being turned over, carried around the dark room. Now, two monks walking home in the rain, Tanzan and Ekido. The water is high and the road is a mess, and at the crossing stands a young woman in a silk kimono who can't get across. Tanzan does something his companion will not stop thinking about for hours.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING, REPLAYING.` → `TANZAN AND EKIDO.` → `A WOMAN WHO CAN'T CROSS.`

segments.voice: Tanzan doesn't hesitate. Come on, he says. He picks her up, carries her across the water, sets her down on the other side, and walks on. Ekido says nothing, all afternoon, all the way to the temple. But he's boiling. These monks had vowed to keep their distance from women, and his companion just picked one up in the road. That night he can't hold it in. We monks aren't supposed to go near women, he says. Especially not young and lovely ones. Why did you do that? And Tanzan answers: I set her down at the river. Are you still carrying her? A word on the details: in the twentieth-century English telling, the crossing is a flooded, muddy road; later retellings made it a river, and the river stuck. Tanzan is remembered as a real Zen teacher with a habit of breaking conventions. Now look who's really carrying the woman. Tanzan held her for a minute, to help, and let her go. Ekido never touched her, and he carried her for hours in his head, heavier with every step. The weight wasn't in the act. It was in the holding on. The old insult. The awkward moment. The thing you should have said. The thing that was done, and finished, long ago. Zen teachers have a word for letting go: hōge, casting down.

45.title: Is that so?
45.hook: Hakuin is wrongly blamed for a child, raises him, is later cleared, and says only "is that so?" (Zen story, Japan)
45.carry: the child in front of you
45.howItsDone: Zen teachers tell the story of Hakuin's "is that so?" to describe equanimity, meeting praise and blame alike, and Rinzai Zen tradition remembers Hakuin as a teacher who renewed it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hōge, letting go: Tanzan set the woman down at the river, and Ekido carried her all day. Your line was I set her down at the river.

segments.voice: Somebody gets you wrong. A rumor at work. A friend who believes the worst. A comment online from someone who's never met you. And the speech starts writing itself: let me explain, you don't understand, how dare you. Now meet Hakuin, a Zen teacher and painter of Japan, whom Rinzai Zen tradition honors as one of its great masters. One morning, the story goes, angry parents bang on his door, holding a newborn baby, and accuse him of something he never did.
screen: `SOMEONE GOT YOU WRONG.` → `LET ME EXPLAIN!` → `HAKUIN AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: A young woman in the village is pregnant, and won't say who the father is. Her parents press her, and finally she names Hakuin, the monk up the road. When the baby is born, the furious parents carry it to his door. This is yours, they say. Take it. And Hakuin says only: is that so? He takes the baby. His good name is gone. People who bowed to him in the road now look away. He asks the neighbors for milk, and cares for the child. He doesn't argue or explain. A year later, the young mother can't bear it anymore. She tells her parents the truth: the father is a young man who works at the fish market. The parents run back up the road, full of shame, apologizing, begging to take the child home. Hakuin hands the baby back. And he says: is that so? Nobody can say for certain this happened; it's a story told about Hakuin, not a record. But look at what those three words do. They aren't agreement: he never says yes, it's mine. And they aren't a fight. They just receive the news. Blame arrives, and he meets it the same way he meets praise. And in between, the thing that needed doing, caring for a baby, got done. It's easy to spend everything on the story about you. Hakuin spent his on the child in front of him. That's the hard part, and the free part.

46.title: The moon can't be stolen
46.hook: the hermit Ryokan gives a thief his clothes and wishes he could give him the moon (Zen story, Japan)
46.howItsDone: Ryokan is remembered in Japan as a poet-monk of simple living, and Zen teachers tell the story of the thief and the moon when talking about generosity and letting go of possessions.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Hakuin, who met blame and apology with the same three words: is that so. Your line was the child in front of you.

One room. A straw roof. A bowl, a cushion, a few poems written on scraps of paper. That was the hut of Ryokan, a Zen monk and poet who lived alone at the foot of a mountain in Japan. Tradition remembers him playing with the village children and begging for his rice, and his poems are still read today. One evening, while Ryokan is out walking, a thief slips into the hut, looking for something to steal. There is nothing. Then Ryokan comes home, and finds him.
screen: `ONE ROOM, A STRAW ROOF.` → `RYOKAN, MONK AND POET.` → `A THIEF IN THE EMPTY HUT.`

segments.voice: Ryokan isn't angry. He's sorry. You've come such a long way to visit me, he says, and you shouldn't go home empty-handed. Please, take my clothes. He takes off the robe he's wearing and hands it over. The thief, bewildered, grabs the clothes and runs off into the dark. Ryokan sits down, naked, in his doorway, and looks up. The moon is rising, huge and bright. And he says to himself: poor fellow. I wish I could have given him this beautiful moon. The story is usually tied to a short poem Japanese tradition credits to Ryokan: the thief left it behind, the moon in my window. Scholars can't say for sure the robbery happened just this way, but the poem and the story have traveled together for a long time. Now look at what Ryokan knows. The thief came for things. Ryokan barely had any, and gave away the last of them without a fight. What he treasured, the thief couldn't carry off, because it wasn't his to keep in the first place. The moon doesn't belong to anyone. It shines on the hut and the thief's road the same. Ryokan's wish is the whole teaching: he wants the thief to have what he himself has. Not the robe. The seeing. The quiet. A night bright enough to be rich in. Things can be guarded carefully, and still be lost. The moon stays.

segments.voice: Think of something you have that no one could steal, a view you love, a memory, a skill, the fact that you're breathing, and rest in it. Then think of one small thing you could give with nothing asked back: a coat you don't wear, your time, a kind word to someone who didn't earn it. Let it go already, in your mind, the way Ryokan let go of his robe.
Ryokan. A Zen monk and poet who gave a thief his clothes, and wished he could give him the moon too.
Your line: the moon stays. Ryokan never counted the robe as lost. That's day forty-six.

47.title: Wash your bowl
47.hook: a new monk asks for teaching, Zhaozhou asks if he's eaten, and says: then wash your bowl (Gateless Gate, case 7)
47.howItsDone: In Zen monasteries, meals are eaten in silence from a set of nested bowls that each monk cleans at the table, and daily work like cooking and cleaning is treated as part of practice, not a break from it.

Sign up for the class, join the gym, open the book everyone talks about, and on the first day it's tempting to walk in ready for the big secret. Tell me the thing. The real thing. The key. Now, a young monk in China, more than a thousand years ago, does exactly that. He's just entered the monastery. He finds the old master, Zhaozhou, one of the most famous teachers in the history of Zen, and asks, earnestly: I've just arrived. Please, teach me. And Zhaozhou asks him about breakfast.
screen: `TELL ME THE REAL THING.` → `A NEW MONK ARRIVES.` → `PLEASE, TEACH ME.`

segments.voice: This one comes from a real book: the Gateless Gate, a collection of forty-eight short Zen cases gathered in China in the twelve hundreds by a monk named Wumen. It's case seven, only a few lines long. The monk says: I've just entered the monastery. Please teach me. Zhaozhou asks: have you eaten your rice porridge? The monk says: yes, I have. And Zhaozhou says: then wash your bowl. The book says the monk understood. No lecture. No secret. The monk wanted something special, and Zhaozhou pointed him at the dishes. Here's what makes it more than a brush-off. In a Zen monastery, washing your bowl isn't a chore you do before the practice starts. It is the practice. Eat when you eat. Wash when you wash. Do the next plain thing completely, with your whole attention, instead of reaching past it for something grander. Zen kept saying this, in many voices. The Japanese teacher Dogen, who studied in China and came home in 1227, wrote a whole set of instructions for the monastery cook, and treated washing rice and scrubbing pots as seriously as sitting in the meditation hall. And notice what Zhaozhou didn't say. He didn't call the porridge unimportant, or tell the monk to hurry past breakfast to the real teaching. He sent him back to the bowl he'd just used. The teaching isn't hidden somewhere else. It's in your hands, in the warm water, in the bowl. You don't need a mountain or a retreat. A sink and one dish are enough.

48.title: The finger and the moon
48.hook: a teaching points at something, so don't stare at the pointing finger (a Buddhist image, Surangama Sutra, much used in Zen)
48.howItsDone: Zen teachers use the finger and the moon to remind students that sutras, koans and talks point toward direct experience, and study in Zen is paired with sitting practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Zhaozhou, who answered a plea for teaching with: then wash your bowl. Your line was eat when you eat.

Point across the room at a ball, for a small child or a puppy, and sometimes all they look at is your finger. They grab it, even. The ball sits there, ignored, while they stare at your hand, waiting for it to do something. It's sweet in a toddler. It's less funny when grown-ups do it, with words and books instead of hands. There's an old picture for this in the Buddhist world, and Zen teachers took it up. Someone points at the moon. And the other person looks at the finger.
screen: `POINT AT THE BALL.` → `THEY LOOK AT YOUR FINGER.` → `SOMEONE POINTS AT THE MOON.`

segments.voice: The picture appears in a Mahayana Buddhist scripture called the Surangama Sutra. The Buddha is talking with his cousin and attendant Ananda, who, tradition says, had heard a great many teachings and could recall them. And the Buddha tells him, more or less: when someone points at the moon to show it to you, follow the finger and look at the moon. If you look at the finger and take it for the moon, you lose the moon. And you lose the finger too, because you've mistaken what a finger is for. That last part is sharp. A finger is for looking past. Zen took this image and ran with it. A later Chan story tells of the teacher Huineng, who, tradition says, couldn't read, being asked by a nun how he could understand scriptures he couldn't even read. The older sources have him answer that the truth doesn't depend on written words, and popular retellings put this picture in his mouth: the truth is like the moon, and words are like a finger. You can see the moon without the finger. Here's why it matters beyond Zen. Every teaching points. Words, books, rituals, even these lessons. They're fingers. They're precious, and worth studying, and they are not the thing. The danger is falling in love with the pointing: memorizing the words, arguing about the finger's shape, collecting fingers, and missing the moon, which is right there, and was the point. So when you hear a teaching, ask: what is this pointing at?

49.title: The strawberry
49.hook: chased by a tiger, hanging from a vine over another tiger, a man tastes a wild strawberry (Buddhist parable, as retold in Zen)
49.howItsDone: Zen teachers retell the strawberry parable to point at full attention in the present moment, and some meditation teachers use mindful eating, tasting one small thing slowly, as a practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was zhǐ yuè: someone points at the moon, and the trick is not to stare at the finger. Your line was not the finger. Today, the last of the Zen week.

A man is walking across a field when he hears it: a growl. A tiger, coming fast. He runs. He reaches the edge of a cliff, grabs the root of a wild vine, and swings himself over the edge. For a moment he's safe. He hangs there, breathing hard. The tiger paces above him, sniffing. He looks down. Far below, a second tiger is waiting for him to fall. And then two mice, one white and one black, come out and begin, little by little, to gnaw through the vine.
screen: `A TIGER, COMING FAST.` → `A VINE OVER THE CLIFF.` → `TWO MICE, GNAWING.`

segments.voice: Then he sees it. Growing out of the cliff face, just within reach: a wild strawberry, red and ripe. Holding the vine with one hand, he picks it with the other. And the story ends: how sweet it tasted! That's the Zen telling, and it stops right there, on the sweetness, without rescuing him. The story has older roots. An Indian parable tells of a man hanging in a well over a monster, with honey dripping into his mouth. It appears in Buddhist writings, in the Hindu epic the Mahabharata, and it traveled west too, into the medieval Christian legend of Barlaam and Josaphat. The older tellings read it as a warning: the mice are day and night, eating through a life's time, and the honey is the pleasure that distracts from the danger. The Zen retelling turns it around. The tigers are still there. The mice still gnaw. Nothing is fixed. But in the middle of all that, there is a strawberry, and he tastes it completely. Not in spite of the danger, and not by ignoring it. Right there, knowing. Everyone is on the vine. Nobody gets off the cliff. You could spend the whole time staring up at one tiger and down at the other, or notice what's growing right in front of you. Look back at this whole week. The cup, emptied. The woman, set down at the river. Is that so. The moon that stays. The bowl, washed. The finger and the moon. And now, one strawberry. Seven Zen stories, each pointing at the same place: right here.
